earlier_scan.source_named: Blissymbols is an artificial graphical symbol system with no spoken phonology; Glottolog langdoc lists zero references of any doctype.

new_statements.quote: Blissymbolics is a concept-based language which makes morphemic use of graphic entities. Spoken languages make morphemic use of sounds; sign languages make morphemic use of hand positions, locations, and movements. (Morpheme is a linguistic term which refers to the smallest units of meaning in a language.)
new_statements.citation: Blissymbolics Communication International (BCI). 2004 [reissued 2020-06-16]. The fundamental rules of Blissymbolics: creating new Blissymbolics characters and vocabulary. Clause 4.0 'Graphic aspects of the language', p. 4.
new_statements.locator: clause 4.0, p. 4 (p. 5 of 30; page footer '©2004 Blissymbolics Communication International Page 4')
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (the PDF's metadata: 30 pp., author field Michael Everson, created 2004-09-28, modified 2020-06-16). extracted text gives the page whose footer reads '©2004 Blissymbolics Communication International Page 4'; clause '4.0 Graphic aspects of the language.' is there and the four sentences quoted by the compiler ('Blissymbolics is a concept-based language which makes morphemic use of graphic entities. Spoken languages make morphemic use of sounds; sign languages make morphemic use of hand positions, locations, and movements. (Morpheme is a linguistic term which refers to the smallest units of meaning in a language.)') appear word for word, only the line breaks differing. Same text at line…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Blissymbols is a purely graphic (ideographic) constructed system: its minimal meaningful units are drawn shapes, not sounds, so it has no phonology and therefore no word stress. The source does not use the word 'stress'; the 'no word stress' reading is an entailment of its statement that the language has no phonic medium (corroborated second-hand by Wikipedia's paraphrase of Bliss 1965: 89–90, 'conceived as a written language with no phonology').
new_statements.exceptions: Bliss 1965 (per Wikipedia, pp. 89–90) allowed that a set of international spoken words could be adopted 'as a travelling aid only'; no such spoken form is standardized by BCI and none has a described phonology. Users read Blissymbols aloud in their own ambient spoken language (e.g. English, Swedish), whose stress is that language's, not Blissymbols'.
new_statements.domain_note: Graphic system only; no word/phrase phonology exists. Statement is about the language as a whole, not about citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: blis1239 / zbl is Blissymbols (Blissymbolics, Semantography), a constructed ideographic graphic system invented by Charles K. Bliss (1949), now standardized by Blissymbolics Communication International; Glottolog classes it as 'Artificial Language'. It has no spoken form and no phonology, so it is of the same kind as sign languages for a word-stress catalog: not applicable rather than undescribed. Recommend excluding blis1239 from the spoken-language target denominator.

Secondary. Lead: 'the characters do not correspond at all to the sounds of any spoken language.' Section 'The speech question': 'Blissymbolics was conceived as a written language with no phonology, on the premise that "interlinguistic communication is mainly carried on by reading and writing"', citing Bliss 1965: 89–90, where Bliss allows a set of international words 'as a travelling aid only'.

sources.citation: Blissymbolics Communication International (BCI). 2004 [reissued with revision note 2020-06-16]. The fundamental rules of Blissymbolics: creating new Blissymbolics characters and vocabulary. 30 pp. www.blissymbolics.org
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent (a full-text search for stress/accent/phon/pronunc: only the acute-accent-in-gloss note and 'parts of speech'). Clause 4.0, p. 4 states the language makes morphemic use of graphic entities whereas spoken languages make morphemic use of sounds — i.e. no phonological medium at all.
